entry: English stage and screen actor. Pleasence began on the West End stage before a screen career that included a 1954 [[BBC]] adaptation of [[George Orwell]]'s *Nineteen Eighty-Four*. He developed a reputation for nervy, unstable characters, including Ernst Stavro Blofeld in *You Only Live Twice* (1967). He played Dr. Samuel Loomis in *Halloween* (1978) and four of its sequels, and later collaborated twice with director [[John Carpenter]]. He won a Drama Desk Award for his stage work.

American politician and diplomat, 13th and 21st U.S. secretary of defense. He served as secretary of defense from 1975 to 1977 under Gerald Ford and again from 2001 to 2006 under George W. Bush, becoming both the youngest and the oldest person to hold the post. Earlier he was an [[Illinois]] congressman and White House chief of staff. He played a central role in the [[2003 invasion of Iraq]], where he claimed Iraq had an active weapons of mass destruction program, but no stockpiles were ever found. His second tenure was controversial, including over the [[Abu Ghraib torture and prisoner abuse|Abu Ghraib torture and prisoner abuse scandal]].

Canadian actor. With a career spanning six decades, Sutherland appeared in films including *Klute* (1971), *Don't Look Now* (1973), *Invasion of the Body Snatchers* (1978) and *Ordinary People* (1980). He won a Primetime Emmy Award for his role in the [[HBO]] thriller *Citizen X* (1995). Considered one of the best actors never nominated for an Academy Award, he received an Academy Honorary Award in 2017. He was a vocal anti-war activist during the [[Vietnam War]].

American businessman and [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] politician, 45th (2017–2021) and 47th president of the United States. He became president of his family's real estate business in 1971, renamed it the Trump Organization, and hosted the television series *The Apprentice* (2004–2015). He won the 2016 election against [[Hillary Clinton]]. After losing the 2020 election to [[Joe Biden]], he refused to concede and tried to overturn the result, an effort that led to the January 6 Capitol attack in 2021. He was impeached twice and acquitted by the Senate both times. In May 2024 he was found guilty in New York state court on 34 counts of falsifying business records, the first U.S. president convicted of a felony. He won the 2024 election against [[Kamala Harris]]. His administration's actions have drawn over 550 lawsuits challenging their legality. Many of his comments and actions have been characterized as racist or misogynistic, and scholars and historians ranked him as one of the worst presidents in American history after his first term.

Polish politician and historian, prime minister of Poland (2007–2014; since 2023). He co-founded the Civic Platform (PO) in 2001 and led it for many years, and he was President of the European Council from 2014 to 2019. He led the European People's Party from 2019 to 2022 and returned to Polish politics in 2021 to lead the Civic Platform again. Elected prime minister for a third time in December 2023, he has focused on reforming the judiciary and warming relations between Poland and the EU. He is the longest-serving prime minister of the Third Polish Republic.

Italian Renaissance sculptor. Born in Florence, he studied classical sculpture and developed an Early Renaissance style, working in stone, bronze, wood, clay, stucco and wax. His bronze *David* was the first freestanding nude male sculpture since antiquity, and like much of his work it was commissioned by the Medici family. He also produced architectural reliefs for pulpits, altars and tombs, and worked in Rome, Padua and Siena. Described as amiable but poor at business, he accepted more commissions than he could handle, like [[Michelangelo]] in the next century, and many works were completed late, handed to other sculptors, or never produced.

Historical and economic region in eastern Ukraine. The name derives from Donets Basin, an abbreviation of Donets Coal Basin, and the region has been an important coal mining and industrial area since the late 19th century. The city of [[Donetsk]] is considered its unofficial capital. Pro-Russian separatist unrest from 2014 split the region into Ukrainian-held territory, about two-thirds, and separatist-held territory, about one-third. Most of the region is occupied by Russia as a result of the [[Russo-Ukrainian war]], and Russia declared its annexation of Donbas in September 2022.

Turkish dish of meat cooked on a vertical rotisserie. Seasoned meat stacked in an inverted cone is slowly turned beside a vertical cooking element, and the cook slices thin shavings from its outer layer. The vertical rotisserie was invented in the 19th-century [[Ottoman Empire]], and related dishes such as [[Shawarma|shawarma]] and Greek gyros derive from it. The sandwich form was popularized in 1970s [[Berlin|West Berlin]] by Turkish immigrants and became a worldwide [[Fast food|fast food]].

City (pop., 2022 est.: 901,645) in eastern Ukraine, center of Donetsk Oblast. Founded in 1869 by Welsh businessman John Hughes around a steel plant and coal mines, it was named Yuzovka after him and renamed Donetsk in 1961. It remains a center of coal mining and [[Steel|steel]] production and is the unofficial capital of the [[Donbas]]. Since 2014 it has been a major site of fighting in the [[Russo-Ukrainian war]]; pro-Russian separatists have administered it as the capital of the Donetsk People's Republic. As of June 2026, Russia has full control of the city. In 2012 a UN report ranked it among the world's fastest depopulating cities.

Domesticated equine used mainly as a working animal. Donkeys derive from the African wild ass and were domesticated in Africa some 5,000–7,000 years ago. The donkey may be classified as *Equus africanus asinus* or as the species *Equus asinus*. More than 40 million donkeys exist worldwide, mostly in underdeveloped countries, where they serve as draught or pack animals. An adult male is a jack and an adult female a jenny. Jacks are often mated with female [[Horse|horses]] to produce [[Mule|mules]]. The word donkey gradually replaced ass in common English use from the 18th century. In the United States, burro is commonly applied to the feral donkeys that live west of the Rocky Mountains.

American singer and songwriter known as the "Queen of Disco." Her single "Love to Love You Baby" reached number 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1976, and "I Feel Love" (1977), recorded with producers Giorgio Moroder and Pete Bellotte, has been hailed as one of the most important records in pop music history. She was the first female artist to record three number one singles in one calendar year, in 1979. Her career slowed amid a late-1970s backlash against [[Disco|disco]], but she returned to the charts in 1983 with "She Works Hard for the Money." She was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2013.

[[Hong Kong]] actor, filmmaker, martial artist and action director. He is best known for portraying the Wing Chun master Ip Man in the *Ip Man* film series (2008–2019), and is credited with popularizing Wing Chun in China. He starred in *Drunken Tai Chi* (1984) and played the antagonist opposite [[Jet Li]] in *Once Upon a Time in China II* (1992), and he made his American debut in *Highlander: Endgame* (2000). He directed *Legend of the Wolf* (1997) and is also known for incorporating [[Mixed martial arts|mixed martial arts]] elements into his action choreography.

Scottish musician, songwriter and record producer. Emerging from the British folk scene in 1965, he scored international hits in the late 1960s, including "Sunshine Superman," which topped the Billboard Hot 100 for one week in 1966. His work blended folk, pop, psychedelia and jazz. He taught [[John Lennon]] a finger-picking guitar style that Lennon used on "Dear Prudence" and other songs. He moved permanently to Ireland in 1994 and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2012.

First-person shooter video game (1993) for MS-DOS, developed and published by id Software. The player is a space marine fighting undead humans and [[Demon|demons]] from the moons of Mars to [[Hell]]. It was an early example of 3D graphics in video games and has been termed the "father" of first-person shooters. Released as shareware, it sold an estimated 3.5 million copies by 1999. In 2007 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for preservation as one of the first 10 "game canon" video games.

Symbol of the estimated likelihood of a human-made global catastrophe, which is represented by midnight. Maintained since 1947 by the nonprofit *Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists*, the clock is reassessed each January. Its main factors are nuclear warfare, [[Climate change|climate change]] and [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]]. The clock was first set at seven minutes to midnight. Its farthest setting was 17 minutes in 1991, and its closest was 85 seconds in 2026.

Hinged or otherwise movable barrier that allows entry into and exit from an enclosure. A door's primary purpose is [[Security|security]] by controlling access to the doorway, or portal. Conventionally a door is a panel fitted to a doorway and hung on hinges, though it may also slide, fold or counterbalance. Doors may also provide [[Privacy|privacy]], separate areas, admit light, control ventilation, reduce noise and block the spread of [[Fire|fire]]. The earliest recorded doors appear in Egyptian tomb paintings, and the most ancient were made of [[Wood|timber]]. Doors can also carry symbolic meaning; receiving a key can signify a change in status from outsider to insider.

India's state-owned public [[Television|television]] broadcaster, abbreviated DD. Established by the [[Government of India]] on September 15, 1959, it is owned by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and is one of the two divisions of Prasar Bharati. It held a monopoly on Indian television until the early 1990s. Its serials, such as *Ramayan* (1987–1988), reached huge audiences. During the 1975–1977 Emergency it broadcast over 170 addresses by [[Indira Gandhi]] while excluding opposition viewpoints. According to Mitra, its programming in the 1980s promoted a homogeneous image of India as a North Indian, Hindu, Hindi-speaking nation.

Organic catecholamine, both a [[Neurotransmitter|neurotransmitter]] and a hormone. In the brain it is synthesized from L-DOPA and released by neurons along several pathways, one of which plays a major role in reward-motivated behavior. Popular culture often portrays dopamine as the chemical of pleasure, but current pharmacological opinion holds that it confers motivational salience, signaling the desirability or aversiveness of an outcome. Outside the central nervous system it acts locally, affecting blood vessels, the kidneys and the pancreas. Loss of dopamine-secreting neurons causes [[Parkinson's disease]], and most antipsychotic drugs used to treat [[Schizophrenia|schizophrenia]] are dopamine antagonists. Injected dopamine treats severe [[Heart failure|heart failure]] or cardiogenic shock.

Use of banned performance-enhancing drugs by athletes as a way of cheating. The World Anti-Doping Code defines doping as one or more anti-doping rule violations, and most international sports organizations, including the International Olympic Committee, prohibit it as unethical. The main reasons for the ban are the health risks of the drugs, equality of opportunity among athletes and the example that drug-free sport sets for the public. Anti-doping authorities say doping goes against the "spirit of sport." Its use dates back centuries; in [[Ancient Rome]], where chariot racing was popular, athletes drank herbal infusions before races. In 1807 the British endurance walker Abraham Wood said he had used laudanum to stay awake for 24 hours during a race.

Supernatural double of a living person, usually perceived as a harbinger of bad luck. In fiction and folklore it is either a [[Ghost|ghost]] or a paranormal phenomenon that haunts the person it duplicates, and literary examples include the evil twin of the protagonist. The word is German, meaning "double-walker," and English usually writes it without the umlaut. In ancient Egyptian belief the *ka* was a tangible spirit double with the same memories and feelings as its person. In [[Norse mythology]], a vardøger is a ghostly double seen performing a person's actions in advance. Many majority-Muslim countries have the *karin* or *qareen*, a spirit double that can be benevolent or harmful.

Change in the frequency, or period, of a wave for an observer moving relative to the wave's source. Named after Christian Doppler, who proposed it in 1842, it explains the change of pitch heard as a vehicle approaches and recedes. A source moving toward the observer compresses successive wave cycles and raises the frequency; a receding source lowers it. For waves in a vacuum, such as light, only relative velocity matters, but for [[Sound|sound]] the speed of the medium also counts. In 1845 Buys Ballot confirmed the effect for sound, and Hippolyte Fizeau found it for light in 1848. In astronomy it measures the radial velocities of stars, and in medicine [[Ultrasound|Doppler ultrasound]] assesses blood flow.

Japanese [[Manga|manga]] series, and the franchise built around it. A blue, earless robotic cat from the 22nd century travels back in time to help Nobita Nobi, a lazy but kind 10-year-old, using gadgets from his four-dimensional pocket. First serialized in 1969 and collected in 45 volumes, the manga spawned three [[Anime|anime]] television series and more than 40 animated films. As of 2024 it had sold over 300 million copies worldwide. In 2008 the title character was appointed Japan's first "anime ambassador" by the Foreign Ministry.

American singer and actress known for her girl-next-door image and distinctive singing voice. She was one of the most popular singers of the 1940s and 1950s and one of the biggest box-office stars of the 1960s. Her recording of "Que Sera, Sera" became her signature song. She co-starred with [[Rock Hudson]] in *Pillow Talk* (1959), for which she was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actress, and worked with [[James Garner]] on *Move Over, Darling* (1963). After ending her film career in 1968 she starred in the sitcom *The Doris Day Show*. A prominent animal welfare advocate, she founded the Doris Day Animal League.

Small, mostly nocturnal [[Rodent|rodent]] of the family Gliridae. Dormice live in Africa, Asia and Europe and are named for their long [[Hibernation|hibernation]], which in temperate zones can last six months or more. There are nine genera and 28 living species, half of them in the African genus *Graphiurus*. Largely arboreal and omnivorous, dormice are unique among rodents in lacking a cecum. They usually breed once, or occasionally twice, a year, with litters averaging four young. The European edible dormouse was considered a delicacy in ancient Rome and is still a delicacy in [[Slovenia]] and parts of [[Croatia]]. The woodland dormouse is the species most often seen in the pet trade, although dormice remain uncommon as pets.

English chemist and pioneer of X-ray crystallography. Hodgkin used the technique to determine the structure of biomolecules, work that became essential to structural biology. She confirmed the structure of [[Penicillin|penicillin]] and mapped that of [[Vitamin B12|vitamin B12]], and in 1964 she received the [[Nobel Prize]] in Chemistry, becoming the third woman to win it. She is the only British woman scientist to have won a Nobel Prize. She was born in Cairo, Egypt, the oldest of four daughters, and her interest in crystals was first displayed at the age of 10. She also elucidated the structure of [[Insulin|insulin]] in 1969, after 35 years of work.
